job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Carla Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I graduated in civil engineering from Sheffield in the summer, and in September I started as a junior drainage designer at a consultancy in Birmingham. Most days I'm drawing pipe layouts for new housing estates on CAD software, checking levels against a spreadsheet, and sitting in on calls where I mostly listen. I share a flat with two girls from my course, and my sister Abena, who's a nurse, comes round on Sundays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the days I'm on site with a hard hat, seeing a trench I drew actually get dug. What wears me out is the pace in the office, because my team lead keeps adding drawings and nobody says no. I also still owe about 22,000 for the degree, and that sits at the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, good, nothing to see here. We already have software that checks pipe gradients, and it saves me an hour a week at most. I'd still want the firm to put in writing that it won't use that saved hour to hand me more drawings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel a bit relieved, because I like how my job works now. I can still see a path from junior to chartered engineer in about five years, and that's the whole plan. The thing I worry about is my debt and my rent, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I do, and I'd keep paying 180 a month off the loan. I'd also finish the chartership paperwork this year, because the earlier I start logging hours, the better. I won't touch any AI tool unless my boss orders me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. A bit tired, because the rent in Birmingham keeps creeping up even when nothing else changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if the rent went up again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my train trips home to see my mother, which I hate saying. I'd rather skip the streaming and the takeaways first, though, and I'd ask my landlord to freeze it. Our building is owned by a company that never fixes the heating, so I wouldn't expect much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, since the senior engineers have been there twenty years. I'd keep an eye on the part-time admin woman, Priya, because she does the filing that software already half does. Nobody's said anything, though.

say: I'd say it's **hype** and I'm glad, because I like how my job works now.
I'd tell friends the firm should promise in writing that saved time won't mean **more drawings**.
think: Privately I'm relieved, because my plan to become **chartered** in five years still looks sound.
My real worry is **rent and student debt**, not machines.
do: Keep paying **180 a month** towards the loan and logging hours for chartership.
Refuse any **AI tool** unless my boss orders me to use one.
feel: Steady, but **tired** from rent creeping up.
S0.quote: I'd still want the firm to put in writing that it won't use that saved hour to hand me more drawings.
fieldNote: She treats the plateau as good news and worries about **rent and debt** instead of machines, which is typical of her.
Her say and think match closely; the only gap is her quiet worry about a colleague's filing job.

steps.text: Keep drawing drainage layouts and log chartership hours every week
Pay 180 a month towards the student loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast and the firms are using it as an excuse. Our company has already stopped hiring a second graduate, and the managing director called it efficiency. I'd put that on every group chat I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it scares me, because drawing standard drainage layouts is exactly the writing-and-checking work the card talks about. If software does the first draft, my team lead needs fewer juniors. I'm top of my year with two internships, so I think I'd survive, but I'd be the one doing twice the checking for the same pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union at my firm, which exists on paper and has maybe six members. I'd go to the next meeting and ask for a rule that checked work is signed by a person. I'd also do the one evening course on drainage modelling my firm pays for, because that's a skill software can't sign for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and annoyed. I don't want to learn the new tools, but I don't want to be the only one who didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want to learn the tools. What happens if your team lead asks you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it, grudgingly, on the firm's time and not mine. I'd be the person who always rechecks the output by hand, even if it's slower. My mother cleaned offices for thirty years, and she taught me you don't skip the checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister, the nurse, about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That nursing is safer, and she shouldn't worry for me. I'd also tell her to join her union before anything happens, because people who waited got nothing.

say: I'd say firms are using AI as an **excuse** not to hire a second graduate.
I'd push for a rule that every checked drawing is **signed by a person**.
think: I'm afraid standard drainage layouts are exactly the **first-draft work** software takes first.
Being top of my year probably saves me, but I'd do **twice the checking**.
do: Join the firm's tiny **union**, which has about six members, and ask for the signing rule.
Take the paid evening course in **drainage modelling** this winter.
feel: **Anxious** and annoyed, and unwilling to be the last person to learn the tools.
S1.quote: My mother cleaned offices for thirty years, and she taught me you don't skip the checking.
fieldNote: Her resistance to AI tools is **principled** and comes from her mother's work ethic, not from fear of the software itself.
She turns to **collective action** quickly, which is consistent with her progressive outlook and her distrust of employers.

steps.text: Join the firm's union and attend the next monthly meeting
Ask the union to demand a person signs every checked drawing
Take the evening drainage modelling course the firm pays for
Recheck any software-made layout by hand before sending it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is not enough time for anyone, and the government should be forced to act now. People like my mother can't retrain at sixty. I'd post that and I'd go to a protest if one were organised in Birmingham.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm frightened. Everything I trained for is desk work, and if the AI can do any thinking job better and cheaper, nobody needs a junior at all. Robots take three more years for the site work, but the drawing is gone on the date. I think the loan could outlive my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop all spending that isn't rent and food and put every spare pound in savings, so I'd have six months. I'd ask Abena whether I could move in with her for a while to save rent. I'd go to the union and any local group that's pushing for support for people who lose work, and I'd ring my MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can't sleep when I think about it for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mother that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mother I'm sorry, because my mother paid for my school shoes with cleaning money and now the whole degree might be worthless. I'd say I'm okay, but she'd know I'm lying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go to a protest. Have you ever been to one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, a climate march in Sheffield in my second year. I'd do it again, but I'd want something to protest for, like a guaranteed income or a shorter week, not just against.

say: I'd say two years is **far too short** and the government must act now.
I'd join a protest and **ring my MP** about support for people who lose work.
think: Everything I trained for is **desk work**, so I fear nobody needs a junior at all.
I think the **student loan** could outlive my job.
do: Cut everything except rent and food to build **six months** of savings.
Ask my sister Abena if I can **move in** for a while to save rent.
feel: **Alarmed**, and I can't sleep when I think about it for long.
S2.quote: My mother paid for my school shoes with cleaning money and now the whole degree might be worthless.
fieldNote: Her fear centres on **debt** and her mother's sacrifice rather than on abstract talk about jobs disappearing.
She wants **something to protest for**, such as a guaranteed income, and not only something to protest against.

steps.text: Cut all spending except rent and food
Save every spare pound towards six months of rent
Ask Abena if I can move into her spare room
Write to my MP and join a rally for income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a bit more breathing space, but it's still far too short to retrain a whole country. I'd tell friends to start asking their employers for a plan now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is the one that makes me think hardest. By 2031 I'll be 27, I could be chartered and maybe have a flat deposit, and the AI could erase it. The hands-on part of civil engineering gets another three years, so I might survive as the person on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change my path towards site work, not design. I'd ask my firm for a placement with the site team and get my construction safety card. I'd also try to save a deposit for a small flat faster, because owning something feels safer than renting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than two years, but unsettled. It's like knowing the date of an exam you didn't choose to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why site work in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a drainage trench still needs somebody to look at the ground, and the card says robots for hands-on work come three years later. A machine can draw a pipe, but it can't tell that the clay is wetter than the survey said. That's the bit I like anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you expect to do well in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners of the firm, and I hate that. The people who sign the cheques will be fine, while the ones who drew the pipes won't. That's why I'd keep pushing for the union.

say: I'd tell friends to **ask employers** for a plan now, because five years is still short.
I'd keep pushing at work for the **union** and shared gains.
think: By 2031 I'll be 27, and the AI could erase my **chartership** and flat deposit plans.
Site work gets about **three more years**, so I should shift towards it.
do: Ask my firm for a placement with the **site team** next year.
Get my **construction safety card** and speed up the flat deposit savings.
feel: **Unsettled**, like knowing the date of an exam I didn't choose.
S3.quote: A machine can draw a pipe, but it can't tell that the clay is wetter than the survey said.
fieldNote: She reasons clearly from the **three-year robot gap** to a move towards site work, which she likes anyway.
She blames **owners and employers**, in line with her progressive outlook, and says so with some heat.

steps.text: Ask my firm for a placement with the site team
Get the construction safety card this spring
Save towards a small flat deposit instead of renting forever

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years I'd call manageable, as long as someone is in charge of making it fair. I'd say we should be using the decade to build a safety net and not waiting till it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a decade means I could be thirty-two, with kids maybe, and a career already built. I'd probably be a senior engineer by then, and the AI would be arriving into a job I know really well. That makes me calmer than the other two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on my chartership, take the site team placement, and slowly learn to check AI work, even though I don't like it. I'd also start paying into a union and a pension at the maximum I can afford. If it came close, I'd consider a master's in project management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot calmer. Ten years is long enough to make a plan and still have a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn to check AI work. Isn't that a change from how you feel now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'm not proud of it. If it's ten years, I can accept using it the way I used a calculator, as long as I'm the one who answers for the result. I just don't want to be the guinea pig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your firm offered to train you on it tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes but on paid time. Then I'd write down every mistake it makes and show it to the team, because somebody should keep that record.

say: I'd say ten years is **manageable** if someone makes sure it's fair.
I'd argue we should use the decade to build a **safety net**.
think: By 32 I'd be a **senior engineer**, so the change would arrive in a job I know well.
I'd accept AI like a calculator as long as **I answer** for the result.
do: Finish **chartership** and take the site team placement.
Learn to **check AI output** on paid time and keep a log of its mistakes.
feel: A lot **calmer**; ten years is long enough for a plan and a life.
S4.quote: I can accept using it the way I used a calculator, as long as I'm the one who answers for the result.
fieldNote: The long runway softens resistance; she would **learn AI** but only on paid time.
Mood stays uneasy because **debt and rent** are with her in every scenario.

steps.text: Finish chartership and take the site team placement
Learn to check AI output on paid training time
Consider a part-time project management master's by 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years, no question. In that one there's no time for the loan to be paid, no time for my mother to understand what happened, and no time for anyone in charge to do anything. What would help is a real plan from the government and the firms, something like guaranteed income for people who lose work, plus a union that has power.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not against technology, I'm against nobody being held to account. I'd like someone to say clearly who answers for it when a machine's drawing floods a street.

headlineQuote: I'm not against technology, I'm against nobody being held to account.
portrait: Carla is a 22-year-old **civil engineer** in her first job at a Birmingham drainage consultancy, owing about 22,000 for her degree.
She is top of her class but **never uses AI tools** and treats checking by hand as a point of pride.
Her progressive outlook leads her to **union action and politics** rather than going it alone.
Her fear rises sharply with the 2028 date and eases with a decade, but **rent and debt** keep her uneasy throughout.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries her most, because there'd be no time to repay the loan or for her mother to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: A government plan for **guaranteed income** and a union with real power, so that firms answer for AI mistakes.
